clue.text: Tennis player looking the same when returning

indicators.note: a name that looks unchanged when read in the return direction is spelt identically both ways

blocks.note: a Yugoslav-born American former world number one whose surname reads identically in both directions

explanation.surface: A tennis player who looks the same each time she sends the ball back over the net.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returning' suggests a tennis return, but here it means reading the name from right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: Monica Seles won nine Grand Slam singles titles, so she is a famous example of a tennis player.

clue.text: Job moved to Tunisia

indicators.note: letters that have been moved are shifted into new positions

explanation.surface: Someone has been relocated to North Africa for work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' looks like a link word, but its letters are needed in the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A situation is a post or position of employment, as in 'situations vacant'.

clue.text: Liberal beat a South American animal

blocks.note: to lam is to thrash or beat

explanation.surface: A Liberal politician hits an Andean beast.
explanation.walkthrough: LAM is an informal verb meaning to hit hard.
explanation.definitionFit: The llama is a domesticated pack animal of the Andes in South America.

clue.text: Drinking bout sounds uplifting around middle of Christmas

indicators.note: in a down entry, something lifted up is read from the bottom upwards
around means placed on either side of something else
the middle of a word is its central letter, the one equidistant from both ends

blocks.note: the fifth of nine letters is the centre one

explanation.surface: A boozy festive session sounds cheerful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounds' looks like a homophone signal but is simply a noun; 'uplifting' looks like praise.
explanation.definitionFit: A session is a period of heavy drinking, as in a long session at the pub.

clue.text: US president – he finally turned sweet? False

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word before it
something turned round faces the other way, so read it backwards

blocks.note: pud is British slang for pudding, a dessert

explanation.surface: Did the US president turn into a sweet? Not true.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' here is the British sense of dessert, shortened to PUD.
explanation.definitionFit: Trumped-up charges are invented or fabricated ones, so the phrase means false.

clue.text: Hard cheese keeping hard, however

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it within you

blocks.note: 'tough!' and 'hard cheese!' are both unsympathetic British exclamations meaning bad luck
H for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A firm cheese that stays firm, nonetheless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard cheese' reads as a cheese type but is the British idiom for tough luck.
explanation.definitionFit: Though is used as an adverb meaning nevertheless or however, as in 'it was late, though'.

clue.text: University student with porridge eating at last

indicators.note: something eating another takes it inside itself

blocks.note: L for learner, as on L-plates
porridge is British slang for a prison sentence, which is doing time

explanation.surface: A university student finally gets round to eating breakfast oats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At last' looks like a phrase, but 'at' goes inside TIME and 'last' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ultimate means final or coming at the end, so it is an adjective synonym for last.

clue.text: Errand boy describing a ship's journey

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw a line around it, so one piece encircles another

blocks.note: a page is a boy who runs errands

explanation.surface: A messenger boy tells of a sea voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Describing' looks like telling a story, but in crosswords it can mean drawing around.
explanation.definitionFit: A passage is a journey, especially one by sea, as in working one's passage.

clue.text: Grew peeved with old bust

indicators.note: something bust is broken apart, so the letters are reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone became annoyed at an old sculpted head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' looks like a sculpture but signals breaking up the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To develop is to grow or mature, so developed is the past tense synonym of grew.

clue.text: Drinks in flipping bad mood

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over end to end

blocks.note: a strop is a sulk or fit of temper

explanation.surface: Someone drinks while in a really foul temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British swear word qualifying the mood.
explanation.definitionFit: Port is a fortified wine, so ports are drinks.

clue.text: Queen in light brown dress in ferry?

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the following one

blocks.note: to sport clothes is to wear or dress in them

explanation.surface: The Queen travels on a ferry wearing a tan outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks ferry as an example: a ferry is one kind of transport.
explanation.definitionFit: A ferry is a vessel carrying passengers, so it is an example of transport.

clue.text: Spanish golfer by Turnberry's third making cut

indicators.note: third picks out the letter in position three of the named word

blocks.note: Seve Ballesteros, the Spanish golfing great

explanation.surface: A Spanish golfer at the Turnberry course makes the cut.
explanation.walkthrough: Turnberry is a Scottish links course that has hosted the Open; making the cut is a golf term.
explanation.definitionFit: To sever is to cut through or cut off.

clue.text: Wonderful American mother with pizzazz

explanation.surface: A lively American mum is marvellous.
explanation.definitionFit: Amazing and wonderful are both adjectives for something astonishingly good.

clue.text: Shilling found in beers after this writer's complaint

indicators.note: something found in another sits inside it

blocks.note: s was the abbreviation for the shilling, an old British coin worth twelve pence

explanation.surface: A writer grumbles at finding a coin in the beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' looks like a grumble, but is meant medically.
explanation.definitionFit: Complaint can mean an illness, and measles is an infectious childhood disease.

clue.text: Child actually has name for chapter

indicators.note: one letter is put in place of another: an abbreviation for name replaces one for chapter

explanation.surface: A child actually swaps a name for a chapter heading.
explanation.definitionFit: An infant is a very young child, a baby or toddler.

clue.text: Scares female with suitable chickens? Not at first

indicators.note: not at first says the opening letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A woman with the right sort of chickens frightens people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chickens' also suggests cowards, who are easily scared, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: To frighten someone is to scare them, so frightens is the matching verb form.

clue.text: Tries attracting trout primarily with lures

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so take leading letters

blocks.note: the first letter of each word

explanation.surface: An angler tries to catch trout using lures.
explanation.definitionFit: Attempts and tries are both verbs meaning makes an effort to do something.

clue.text: Sir's super new floors

indicators.note: something new has been made over, so its letters come in a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: the letters as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A knight's excellent new floorboards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Floors' looks like a noun about flooring; it is the verb meaning stuns.
explanation.definitionFit: To floor someone is to astonish or stagger them, so it is a verb synonym of surprises.

clue.text: Second best editor cried

blocks.note: the cream is the best of anything

explanation.surface: The runner-up editor broke down in tears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second best' reads as one phrase, but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Cried can mean shouted out loud, which is what someone who screamed did.

clue.text: Bore is sitting in shade

indicators.note: something sitting in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: a shade of meaning is a nuance

explanation.surface: A tedious person sits in the shadow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bore' could be a verb in the past tense; it is the noun for a tiresome person or thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A bore and a nuisance are both nouns for an annoying person or thing.

clue.text: State aid gets eradicated initially? This could be mean

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letters of the words before it

blocks.note: to aver is to state or assert

explanation.surface: If state aid is wiped out, someone could call that mean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' looks like stingy; here it is the arithmetic sense.
explanation.definitionFit: In statistics the mean is the most common kind of average, so an average could be a mean.

clue.text: Left one day in German aircraft

indicators.note: in places the preceding pieces inside the next one

explanation.surface: Someone departed one day in a German plane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like a past-tense verb but is the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A glider is an engineless aircraft that flies on air currents.

clue.text: Missing call almost upset Charles?

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
in a down entry, upset means turned upside down, so read from the bottom up

blocks.note: King Charles III, the British monarch

explanation.surface: A missed phone call has upset Charles.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags Charles as an example of a king.
explanation.definitionFit: Missing and lacking are both adjectives for something absent or not there.

clue.text: Got rid of soft egg on top of dish

indicators.note: in a down entry the top of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: p for piano, the musical direction to play softly
to egg on is to urge

explanation.surface: A soft-boiled egg is placed on top of a dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Egg on' reads as food on a plate; 'egg' alone means urge, while 'on' places it above the last piece in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To purge is to rid oneself of something unwanted, so purged means got rid of.

clue.text: Reach a church – that is half of nave

indicators.note: half of a word keeps only some of its letters, here the back pair

blocks.note: the second half of the word

explanation.surface: Someone gets to a church and finds half the nave.
explanation.walkthrough: The church setting makes 'nave' feel like architecture, but only its letters matter.
explanation.definitionFit: To achieve a goal is to reach or attain it.

clue.text: Somewhat normal to stifle voices

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only part of the following words is used

blocks.note: runs across the end of normal, all of to and the start of stifle

explanation.surface: It is fairly usual to muffle voices.
explanation.definitionFit: Altos are singers of the low female or high male range, i.e. a kind of voice in a choir.

clue.text: Reveal note man found in ancient city

indicators.note: something found in another lies inside it

blocks.note: cove is old British slang for a man or chap
Ur of the Chaldees, the Sumerian city

explanation.surface: A note left by a man is discovered in a ruined city.
explanation.walkthrough: UR is the crossword's favourite ancient city.
explanation.definitionFit: To uncover something is to expose or reveal it.

clue.text: Behold type of painting in V&A

indicators.note: in puts the first piece inside the second

blocks.note: the Victoria and Albert Museum in London

explanation.surface: Look at this kind of painting in a London museum.
explanation.definitionFit: Voila is a French exclamation meaning there it is, used like the command behold.

clue.text: Greek character's itchiest hat regularly removed

indicators.note: removing at regular intervals drops every other letter

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth letters and so on

explanation.surface: A Greek man's hat is so scratchy he takes it off.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after 'character' is read as 'is' joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Theta is the eighth letter of the Greek alphabet, a character in that writing system.

clue.text: Makes bigger figs, I mean bananas

indicators.note: bananas means crazy, so the letters go wild

explanation.surface: A fruit-seller's figs, and bananas, are enlarged.
explanation.walkthrough: Among figs, 'bananas' looks like another fruit; it is the slang for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: To magnify is to enlarge something, so magnifies means makes it bigger.

clue.text: Cook needs spud put aside

indicators.note: to cook ingredients is to mix and alter them

explanation.surface: The chef must have a potato set aside.
explanation.walkthrough: Spud is informal for potato, which fits the kitchen picture.
explanation.definitionFit: To suspend something is to set it aside temporarily, so suspended means put aside.

clue.text: Rabbit crossing river with small rat

indicators.note: something crossing another spans it, holding it inside

blocks.note: to rabbit and to gas are both British slang for chattering on

explanation.surface: A rabbit crosses a stream alongside a little rat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rabbit' and 'rat' look like animals; both are verbs, chatter and inform on.
explanation.definitionFit: To grass is British slang for informing to the police, just as to rat on someone is.
